text:
French coastguards have rescued hundreds of people from a boat that caught fire in the English Channel near the port of Boulogne-sur-Mer.

The local French administration which handles the English Channel and North Sea areas said three coastguard ships rescued 157 from the boat which was carrying migrants on Tuesday morning, local time.

There were no reported casualties.

Migration has been one of Europe's most divisive political issues since a crisis in 2015-16, when more than a million refugees and migrants — many of them fleeing war in Syria — arrived in Europe.

Last week, three people died while trying to cross the Channel on a small boat.

The latest rescue highlights the growing dangers of Channel crossings as human traffickers cram ever larger numbers of migrants onto flimsy boats.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged on Sunday to be "relentless" in curbing small-boat arrivals.

The Channel is one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, and its strong currents have resulted in the deaths of many migrants trying to cross over from France to Britain.

Human traffickers typically overload their dinghies, leaving them barely afloat.

"This incident underlines the terrible dangers of small boat crossings. We continue to work relentlessly with the French and our partners overseas to prevent these perilous journeys," a British government spokesperson said.

The rescue comes shortly after Britain's right-wing Reform UK party framed its plan to stop asylum seekers from entering the country as a key election promise, which it claimed would become the largest military operation in the Channel since World War Two.

EU holds crisis talks over migrant influx

The rescue effort on the English Channel came as European interior ministers met to discuss a mass border rush in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta last week.

About 70,000 of the 72,000 migrants who entered Ceuta had left, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said, adding that the Schengen space was never compromised as the North African enclave is not included in the agreement.

He said fellow European leaders recognised Madrid for its "immediate and efficient" response.

Mr Grande-Marlaska said Spanish intelligence had no indications a mass crossing into Ceuta was imminent.

"There was no report, no warning," he said.

The minister added that Madrid had worked as fast as possible to install a maritime barrier off Ceuta's coast, following a ruling by Spain's Supreme Court in July mandating that migrants who arrived by swimming could not be immediately deported if no barrier was in place.

The influx of migrants prompted a crisis within the European Union, with Italy and Denmark among countries calling for Spain to be excluded from the bloc's free travel scheme.

text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. — Memphis immigration advocates are working to stop ICE deportation flights at Wilson Air Center.

Members of Vecindarios 901 say the transportation of immigrants expedites deportations and violates their rights.

The protestors are joining a nationwide movement against ICE flights, and they’re targeting companies potentially servicing and profiting off what they call “an inhumane system”.

“We want the people in the bus to know we see them as they go by. Letting them know we see them, and we witness their suffering, and we ask for justice,” Joni Laney, an advocate.

Since March, the group has tracked 51 flights leaving Wilson Air Center. They say more than 1,500 people were transported by bus from the West Tennessee Detention Facility to Wilson Air Center, usually destined for Alexandria, Louisiana.

“Twenty-five to thirty mostly Latino men and women are taken off the bus shackled,” said advocate Jim West. “One hour of ICE flight activity costs the taxpayers $17,000. In one day, one ICE airplane will make approximately $119,000 in trips with our taxpayer dollars.”

There was also a moment where protestors read a story about a woman being separated from her family, and being unsure of when she’d see her children.

Organizers of the rally hope to change the way immigrants are treated and end business dealings that they believe could put people at risk.

“You cannot serve both God and money. There is no amount of money that should allow these abuses to continue,” said Liana Venezia, an advocate. “Please do not wait to speak out on this cruelty. Let us choose justice, let us choose mercy, and let us honor the image of God in any person who sets foot in our city.”

text:
HOUSTON, Texas (KTRK) -- The City of Houston and its officers are being sued for holding people at traffic stops to turn them over to Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, according to a lawsuit.

A lawsuit filed this week claims what officers are doing is unconstitutional.

The lawsuit stems from a June traffic stop of 29-year-old Erick Lopez, accused of running a stop sign.

His attorney and family say the Houston police officer held him for two hours until ICE agents arrived because he had a federal administrative immigration warrant. They say Lopez didn't have a criminal history.

"The national crime index computer system put the 700,000 non-criminal warrants in there. Before, they just had criminal warrants in the computer system, so now police can see these non-criminal immigration administrative warrants that aren't about crimes, and that's why he is held," Civil Rights Attorney Randall Kallinen said. "Many people are being held for long periods of time for these administrative warrants. These are not criminal warrants, not decided by a judge."

Houston police policy is vague, but there is no specified time limit for how long officers are required to wait for ICE to arrive.

It says as long as there is a legitimate purpose for the stop, they can hold someone as long as it's reasonably necessary. But what is reasonable?

Attorneys who filed the lawsuit say no time is reasonable under the Constitution.

Constitutional law expert Seth Chandler says in general police can only hold you at a traffic stop for the amount of time it takes to conduct the stop itself. He says if officers find you have a criminal warrant during that stop, they can hold you longer to investigate.

"The question here is whether an immigration warrant, which is not issued by a traditional judge, should be treated the same as an allegation that you were involved in a bank robbery or another violation police observed while conducting the traffic stop," Chandler said.

As this lawsuit is underway, Lopez's attorney says he was undocumented and has been deported back to Honduras.

"Erick's goal is the same. He doesn't want this to happen to anyone," Kallinen said.

Kallinen says he's trying to make this a class action lawsuit because he says there are others who Houston officers have also told during traffic stops to wait on ICE.

text:
In response to increased immigration enforcement measures throughout the country, two U.S. Catholic bishops have issued fresh statements affirming the human dignity of immigrants as children of God and calling for immigration reform.

Both prelates said Americans should understand why people flee their home countries in search of a better life while acknowledging the nation’s right to enforce its immigration laws. The current situation, however, is unjust, immoral, and must be fixed, both men emphasized.

Human dignity

On Aug. 3, the centennial anniversary of the elevation of San Antonio to a metropolitan archdiocese, Archbishop Gustavo García-Siller released a pastoral letter expressing the Church’s solidarity with migrants and calling for the “careful and well-formed moral discernment of every Catholic conscience” in response.

Meanwhile, on Aug. 1, Bishop Robert Gruss of the Diocese of Saginaw, Michigan, issued a statement in which he reminded the faithful of the “inherent human dignity” of every person.

Gruss said the current “challenge” facing the United States, which has “consistently received immigrants, refugees, exiles, and the persecuted from other lands” throughout its history, is “how to deal with a situation when one administration has allowed individuals and families to migrate … freely and the next administration wants their removal.”

The bishop wrote that the removal of “immigrants who have caused harm to society by participating in criminal activity” is understandable, but asked if it is “fair to remove those who are and have been contributing to society in a positive way, oftentimes for many years?”

He said that a “just and civil society” would not allow the deportation or detention of people “without cause” or “meaningful legal representation, without access to family or a supportive community, and without basic human needs being met.”

He urged the faithful to “push for public policy changes that secure civil rights for all immigrants” and “humane border enforcement policies” that simultaneously uphold national security while protecting the “safety and dignity” of those who come to the country to work.

‘We Will Come to You’

García-Siller promulgated his letter, titled “We Will Come to You: United in Solidarity with Our Brothers and Sisters in Migration,” at a Mass at San Fernando Cathedral in downtown San Antonio.

“We are living in a world of war,” the letter began. “Across continents, people are dying every day. Across borders, survivors are forced to migrate. They do not leave by choice, but because of violence, hunger, fear, and oppression.”

In the 56-page letter, composed of five sections and concluding with a prayer to Our Lady of Guadalupe, García-Siller said he prayed “for a long time” before writing, saying he wanted to write from “the right place, one of accompaniment and solidarity.”

He said the letter addresses an “unprecedented” time in the country, writing that “a convergence of structural and legal tactics … calls for the careful and well-formed moral discernment of every Catholic conscience.”

“I write to comfort the afflicted, to ignite the comfortable, and to confront injustice with the full conviction of the Gospel.”

He went on to cite his personal experience of “years walking alongside” migrants, many of whom are living in so much fear they rarely leave their homes, as well as his own story as a migrant himself.

Fear has taken root

The archbishop wrote that he has witnessed a “fear that has taken root” across the archdiocese, saying he and other pastors “pray with parents who embrace their children each morning unsure if they will be home at night,” and describing parents who avoid taking children to the doctor or to go to work “because each mile carries risk.”

“The community bears this cross, and the Church cannot be silent,” he wrote, describing declining Mass attendance and the worsening physical health of those who suffer fear related to immigration.

“The people have not lost their faith,” he wrote. “Many, however, have lost their sense of safety and belonging.”

The Church must “defend the dignity of those caught in the machinery of removal,” he emphasized.

García-Siller described visiting three detention centers in the area, including the South Texas Family Residential Center in Dilley, the largest family detention center in the nation, saying he’s witnessed “firsthand, violations of human dignity within their walls.”

He went on to quote Bishop Steven Biegler of the Diocese of Cheyenne, Wyoming, who wrote in a pastoral letter in April that “‘the current campaign of mass detention and deportations is immoral.’”

‘The Body of Christ does not abandon its members in chains’

García-Siller accused private corporations of profiting from the processing and movement of large numbers of detained immigrants from one site to another.

He also cited an investigation by U.S. Sen. John Ossoff, D-Georgia, which documented more than 1,000 “credible reports of human rights abuses since January 2025, including “medical neglect, denial of food and water, overcrowding, sleep deprivation, and the separation of breastfeeding mothers from their infants,” as well as similar abuses in privately-run sites.

García-Siller called the public narrative that only criminals are being removed “misleading,” writing that “73% of those in immigration detention have no criminal conviction, and only 5% have been convicted of a violent crime.”

He described how pastors, deacons, extraordinary ministers, and trained catechists are developing “active ministries of accompaniment” in the archdiocese, visiting migrants in their homes, bringing the sacraments along with medicines and other supplies, as well as in detention centers.

“If your family has been detained, tell us. We will go to them. The Body of Christ does not abandon its members in chains,” García-Siller declared.

The archbishop went on to lament that existing legal pathways take years to navigate, years that families cannot afford to wait as they seek safety and stability. He called for more accessible legal pathways, saying migrants would take those pathways if they were available. Migrants’ “contribution to the common good of our nation” demands such, he wrote.

At the end of the letter, García-Siller entrusted the situation to Our Lady of Guadalupe, who herself crossed borders of culture and race and walked the road of exile with the Holy Family: “Long before she was Queen of Mexico … she was a mother who crossed a border. She knows this road; she walked it with her own feet.”

(EWTN News)

title: Ceuta border rush: Loved ones in limbo over missing family members | CNN
authors: Hira Humayun, Sarah Hutter, Eyad Kourdi
description:
Since he was last seen in the Moroccan border town on Fnideq that day, nobody has been in contact with him, his sister Mariem says.
“The uncertainty has been devastating for our family.” The family are urging anyone with information regarding his whereabouts — no matter how little — to come forward.
The surge prompted Spain to deploy its military after Ceuta authorities asked for help in managing the mounting border crisis that peaked on Thursday.
“Every day without news increases our fear and sadness.” Like others, they have contacted Moroccan and Spanish authorities, but to no avail.
Fourteen-year-old Nada Shiba was also headed to the Ceuta border crossing with her mother when they got separated and the young teen went missing, her uncle Yousef told CNN.
text:
Omar Lotfi’s family has been crushed under the weight of unanswered questions ever since he went missing.

From pleas on social media to contacting hospitals, aid groups and authorities, they’ve left no stone unturned.

Lotfi, 24, went missing on July 31, after leaving his hometown of Dar Bouazza on the outskirts of the Moroccan city of Casablanca, in the hope of reaching Ceuta. He was among more than 70,000 migrants who last week rushed toward the border with the small Spanish exclave in North Africa in the hope of starting new lives in Europe after a recent Supreme Court ruling on migrant returns.

At least 72 of them died, some drowning and others trampled in the charge. Most of the others have since returned to Morocco, but a few thousand remain, according to the Ceuta government. And among those that remain, some, like Lotfi, remain unaccounted for.

Since he was last seen in the Moroccan border town on Fnideq that day, nobody has been in contact with him, his sister Mariem says.

“We do not know where he is, whether he is safe, whether he was taken to a hospital, detained, or if something else happened,” she told CNN. “The uncertainty has been devastating for our family.”

The family are urging anyone with information regarding his whereabouts — no matter how little — to come forward.

“Omar is not just another missing person. He is a beloved son, brother, and friend,” Mariem said. “He has dreams, hopes, and a family that loves him deeply. Every day without any information about him brings more fear, pain, and uncertainty.”

Omar has tried to cross into Ceuta with a friend, who also hasn’t been heard from, Mariem told CNN. His decision to go caught the family by surprise.

“The emotional pain of not knowing whether our loved one is alive or where he might be is impossible to describe,” she said.

Despite the heartbreak, the Lotfis remain hopeful, praying every day that Omar will come home safe.

Experts say that, alongside the Supreme Court ruling, the relatively strong Spanish economy, a recent program to grant legal status to migrants already in the country and longstanding economic pressures on young people in Morocco and elsewhere in North Africa are factors that encouraged the border rush.

The surge prompted Spain to deploy its military after Ceuta authorities asked for help in managing the mounting border crisis that peaked on Thursday. People breached border fences, swam to the Spanish exclave and were seen running into the territory in scenes described as “absolute chaos” by authorities.

Such scenes have added to the fears of families like the Lotfis — as has the uncertainty. There is still no official figure for the number of people missing. CNN has reached out to the Moroccan government for comment.

Even among those migrants who have contacted their families, there is not necessarily a desire to return.

On Tuesday, Issam al-Mardy heard from his 26-year-old brother Et-Tayeb, who is in Ceuta, without food, shelter … or any plans to return to Morocco. Issam said his brother had been unemployed and had wanted to work in Spain.

“His dream was to go to Europe,” Issam told CNN. “Since he was young, he had been obsessed with Europe.”

CNN has attempted to contact Et-Tayeb directly.

Missing minors

The Ceuta government estimates that of the thousands of migrants that remain, more than 800 are minors.

Abdullah Al-Hafi, 17, is thought to be among them. The last time his family heard from him was when he was heading to Fnideq, Morocco, on July 30.

“Our family is living through a very painful time,” his brother Mohammed said. “Every day without news increases our fear and sadness.”

Like others, they have contacted Moroccan and Spanish authorities, but to no avail. Like other families, they are hoping someone with knowledge of his whereabouts will come forward.

Fourteen-year-old Nada Shiba was also headed to the Ceuta border crossing with her mother when they got separated and the young teen went missing, her uncle Yousef told CNN.

At the border, Nada went through but her mother did not, and ended up coming back — which has stirred tensions within the family.

“I’m very depressed, I’m very stressed about Nada’s fate,” Yousef said. “I have no idea where she is and if she’s OK or not.” His brother Mohammed, Nada’s father, has been traumatized ever since, Yousef said.

“I cannot blame Nada for this because all the youngsters in Morocco know that a better future lies in migrating to Spain, to live in Spain,” he said, adding that the European country’s track record in human rights, democracy and freedom compared to that of Morocco appeals to many Moroccans.

Had Nada been with family and taken care of in Spain, Yousef said he wouldn’t be as distressed as he is. But the thought of his young niece alone, not knowing where she is and how she is doing, outweighs any benefit of being in Spain under current circumstances.

CNN is attempting to contact Nada’s mother.

Rights groups say situations like Nada’s are particularly concerning.

“At this point, what’s important is to make sure that the child does not stop being a child simply because they cross the border,” Save the Children’s director of advocacy and regional development in Spain, Catalina Perazzo, said. “They’re entitled to this individual assessment and a safe place to sleep, to protection from harm and access to this specialized care.”

She warned that the sudden influx had overwhelmed the city and that there were “still a lot of children in distress in the forests, on the streets in Ceuta,” where food, water, shelter and clothing were scarce.

Meanwhile, the Moroccan Association of Human Rights has called on both Moroccan and Spanish authorities to open “independent, urgent and transparent investigations” into the deaths at the crossing and also to help “grieving families to know the fate of their children and recover their bodies for dignified burial.”

For families who have yet to hear from their loved ones, they point out, the unknowns are agonizing.

title: Family seeks investigation after death of Salvadoran man in ICE custody at Delaney Hall
description:
Edwin Lopez-Cornejo died Aug. 1 while being held at Delaney Hall, a privately operated immigration detention facility in Newark.
During a gathering Tuesday, Lopez-Cornejo's family and supporters demanded answers, arguing his death may have been preventable.
Delaney Hall has faced months of protests and scrutiny over the treatment of detainees.
According to ICE, Lopez-Cornejo entered the United States illegally in 2006 and was removed a few months later.
Mikie Sherrill said, in part, "This tragedy is another painful reminder of why Delaney Hall should be closed."
text:
NEWARK, N.J. (WPVI) -- Family members and community advocates are calling for an independent investigation into the death of a Salvadoran man who died while in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody at a Newark, New Jersey, detention center.

Edwin Lopez-Cornejo died Aug. 1 while being held at Delaney Hall, a privately operated immigration detention facility in Newark.

Federal authorities have said Lopez-Cornejo suffered a medical emergency, but the cause of death remains under investigation.

During a gathering Tuesday, Lopez-Cornejo's family and supporters demanded answers, arguing his death may have been preventable.

"I'm going to grow up without a father," Lopez-Cornejo's 12-year-old daughter said.

She later added, "We had so many plans, but I never did them because ... they're just heartless monsters. Shame on all of them."

Family members allege medical negligence related to Lopez-Cornejo's high blood pressure and diabetes. ICE has maintained that Lopez-Cornejo received proper medical care while in custody.

Delaney Hall has faced months of protests and scrutiny over the treatment of detainees. State leaders have continued to seek access to the facility and records related to its operation.

"This will not last forever, and we will hold this administration accountable," said Rep. Analilia Mejia, NJ-11.

According to ICE, Lopez-Cornejo entered the United States illegally in 2006 and was removed a few months later. The agency said he later re-entered the country on an unknown date and was detained June 18.

According to ABC News, Lopez-Cornejo is at least the 23rd detainee to die in ICE custody this year and the second at Delaney Hall.

Community members honored Lopez-Cornejo during a vigil outside the detention center Monday.

In a statement, Gov. Mikie Sherrill said, in part, "This tragedy is another painful reminder of why Delaney Hall should be closed."

Lopez-Cornejo's family is demanding that ICE and GEO Group, which operates the facility, release all medical records related to his detention and treatment.

Sherrill also said her administration would continue pursuing justice and transparency in the case.

text:
A man who has lived in Montana for 10 years and faced pressure from federal authorities to deport himself is among 17 people being illegally detained in the Cascade County Detention Center, according to a federal court filing this week.

Jesus Verde Hernandez, of Worden, faces no criminal charges, but U.S. Customs and Border Patrol stopped him in Lewistown on Thursday, July 30, and arrested him without a warrant, according to his lawyers, with Upper Seven Law of Helena.

The same day, the lawyers asked the court to release him. A news release from the law firm says on Friday, the U.S. District Court of Montana set a hearing for Aug. 5 to consider releasing Hernandez.

Sunday, the lawyers asked the court to certify a class-action case. They argue Hernandez is one of approximately 17 men detained in the Cascade County jail on immigration holds and without criminal charges, and others in Montana are in a similar situation.

“Many class members will be unable to access the court because federal immigration officials will coerce them into self-deporting without adequately informing them of the legal consequences of doing so,” the court filing says.

An order Monday prevents authorities from transporting any of the others out of Montana before an Aug. 18 hearing in Missoula.

The petition was filed against Cascade County Sheriff Jesse Slaughter; Chief U.S. Patrol Agent Zachary Crosson of Havre; U.S. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin; and Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, among other officials.

Slaughter said the Cascade County Detention Center is simply the contract facility for the detainees. An online federal court system did not have the government’s written response filed by Tuesday afternoon.

The filing by the nonprofit law firm asks the Department of Homeland Security to release Hernandez and others it argues were detained without due process. The news release describes Hernandez’s arrest.

For 30 hours, Hernandez was offered only crackers and water, and he was denied the over-the-counter medication he takes to manage chronic pain, the news release said.

The court filing asks the court to immediately release Hernandez and all similar plaintiffs or hold hearings to show they’re a danger or flight risk.

The court filing says Hernandez lives with his partner of 14 years and their three children, 9, 6 and 4; his partner and children all are U.S. citizens; and he is a step-father to his partner’s two children from a previous relationship, both young adults and U.S. citizens.

“Jesus is a devoted father and member of the Worden community,” the court document says. “Recently, for over a year, he and his partner supported and took care of a homeless teen in the community.”

On July 30, Customs and Border Patrol arrested Hernandez and another man in Lewistown without a warrant, the court filing says. It says federal authorities took them to the local police station, “where they remained handcuffed for approximately two hours.”

Then, CBP drove them to Jordan, where they picked up a third detainee, and they took Hernandez and the two others to the Malta Border Patrol Station and incarcerated Hernandez and the others overnight, the court record states.

A news release from the law firm says Customs and Border Patrol pressured Hernandez to sign papers to agree to self-deport.

“Afraid of facing an even more prolonged separation from his family, Jesus felt pressured to sign,” the news release said. “Had his attorneys been unable to reach him, he would have agreed to voluntarily deport under false pretenses.”

On July 31, authorities took Hernandez and the other person arrested in Lewistown to the Cascade County Detention Center, where they remain among 17 men detained there without criminal charges, court records state.

“Jesus seeks to represent a class of noncitizens detained at CCDC or other detention facilities in Montana who, on information and belief, face prolonged, mandatory detention because of a draconian policy adopted by the Department of Homeland Security that prevents them from being released on bond while in lengthy civil immigration proceedings,” the court document said.

The lawyers believe the Department of Homeland Security intends to start removal proceedings for Hernandez and the others and will argue they are subject to mandatory custody — but the policy was declared unlawful by the Ninth Circuit on July 30, 2025.

DHS officials argue that people such as Hernandez aren’t eligible to be released on bond during immigration proceedings, the court filing says.

However, Hernandez’s attorneys point out that the District Court of Montana, the Ninth Circuit, and “the vast majority of courts” have rejected the policy of treating people arrested in the interior of the country — as opposed to at the border — in a way that subjects them to mandatory detention.

“Jesus is neither a danger to the community nor a flight risk,” the court document says. “On information and belief, no other class member is a danger to the community or a flight risk.”

The lawyers allege the continued detention violates the Immigration and Nationality Act and the Due Process Clause of the U.S. Constitution.

They also note in recent months, “there has been a surge of immigration arrests in Montana,” multiple people are seeking relief from “this same unlawful interpretation,” and more petitions are likely to follow unless the court certifies a class-action case.

“Many class members … will be quickly boarded onto vans and planes and sent to neighboring states with ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) facilities and other far-off locations before they have a chance to seek help,” the court filing said, arguing for the necessity of the class.

After the hearing on Aug. 18, the court will determine whether the Department of Homeland Security will release the others being held from detention.

In a statement, Upper Seven Executive Director Rylee Sommers-Flanagan said Hernandez’s arrest is part of a pattern by federal immigration officials.

“And the quick transfer of detained individuals out of state without opportunity to contest their detention or consult with an attorney violates the law. The rule of law is for everyone, and we will fight to uphold it for our fellow Montanans, without exception,” Sommers-Flanagan said in a statement.

title: Private prison in west central Minnesota to reopen for ICE use - InForum
description:
ST. PAUL — The Prairie Correctional Facility, an idle private prison in Appleton, Minnesota, will soon be used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Appleton is in west central Minnesota, about 50 miles from Willmar, and about 150 miles from Fargo, Sioux Falls and the Twin Cities.
The other facility in Minnesota designated for federal immigration purposes is the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building in Fort Snelling.
Federal immigration authorities also have agreements with several county jails to house detainees for longer periods.
CoreCivic also operates the Dilley immigration detention center in Texas, where 5-year-old Liam Ramos was held.
text:
ST. PAUL — The Prairie Correctional Facility, an idle private prison in Appleton, Minnesota, will soon be used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

CoreCivic, a company that owns dozens of immigration detention centers across the country, confirmed Tuesday, Aug. 4, that it has been awarded a contract with ICE. The contract begins Aug. 11 and will last for five years, according to CoreCivic.

"While this facility has been idle since 2010, we have made investments to help ensure an efficient reactivation in the event of a new contract,” CEO Patrick D. Swindle said in the release. “The geographic location of this facility, similar to our other recent contract awards, improves our ability to support our government partner throughout the United States."

Appleton is in west central Minnesota, about 50 miles from Willmar, and about 150 miles from Fargo, Sioux Falls and the Twin Cities. Speculation about ICE using the facility, which houses 1,600 beds, began last summer.

CoreCivic said they expect to begin receiving detainees in the fall or winter of 2026, with the “full ramp” to be completed by the spring or early summer of 2027. The company said it expects a total annual revenue of $75 million.

The other facility in Minnesota designated for federal immigration purposes is the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building in Fort Snelling. Federal immigration authorities also have agreements with several county jails to house detainees for longer periods.

CoreCivic has 81 private facilities across the country, though it’s not clear how many of those are contracted with federal authorities. CoreCivic also operates the Dilley immigration detention center in Texas, where 5-year-old Liam Ramos was held.

Paul Schnell, commissioner of the Minnesota Department of Corrections, has been outspoken about his disapproval of ICE using the Appleton facility, though he did not provide a new comment Tuesday.

“DHS is not claiming Minnesota lacks detention capacity. Rather, it wants to make an example of our state again, detaining people from across the country — individuals with no connection to Appleton and who would be separated from legal counsel, family and meaningful oversight,” he wrote to the Star Tribune in June.

CoreCivic directed further questions regarding the contract to the Department of Homeland Security, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment. When the proposed contract was posted in June, the contract said ICE needed more beds to “meet the administration’s interior enforcement and border decompression goals.”

Tuesday's announcement comes on the heels of Operation Metro Surge, during which Renee Good and Alex Pretti were fatally shot by ICE agents in Minneapolis.

Several Minnesota officials, including Gov. Tim Walz, had not commented on the announcement by early afternoon Tuesday, but AFSCME Council 5 Executive Director Bart Andersen said in a statement that the labor union “strongly condemns” the decision.

“No corporation should generate revenue and profit off imprisoning human beings, separating families, and expanding a for-profit detention system that treats human beings and workers as sources of profit for shareholders,” he said.

text:
Numerous and high-profile false narratives about immigrants’ reliance on public benefits, alleged fraud, and predisposition toward violent crime have enabled the Trump Administration and lawmakers to fund a mass immigrant detention agenda. Since January 2025, Congress and the administration have directed billions of dollars into recruiting more immigration agents, opening and staffing carceral facilities, and increasing the number of immigrant arrests and detentions.

The narratives used to support these actions and policies repackage the same stereotypes and tropes that have enabled divestment from, and the mass incarceration of, Black people in the U.S. As such, we can view these actions by the federal government, complicit local governments, and private corporations as a means to profit from fear and separation by boosting the population of individuals subject to the horrors of imprisonment and enslaved labor.

If the Trump Administration continues down their current path of targeting immigrants, private contractors stand to be among the principal beneficiaries, and the harms will ripple throughout families, communities, and the economy.

Economic Disruption and Forced Labor

Federal officials have called for arrest quotas to fill newly built detention centers, but not because there has been a sudden spike in crime. Indeed, the number of immigrants in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody with no criminal convictions has skyrocketed since January 2025. For the first time, this population outnumbers those who have convictions and pending charges. The vast majority of people who have been taken into ICE custody over the past 18 months face an alleged civil administrative violation, not a criminal charge.

More detainees means a larger captive labor force available for ICE’s “voluntary work program,” which supposedly offers opportunities for detainees to make money, stay out of trouble, and improve detention centers’ operations. However, labor programs within carceral facilities are inherently coercive, and reports indicate that immigrant ICE detainees are forced into intensive manual labor for as little as $0.13 an hour. This practice is aligned with the nation’s long history of economically exploiting incarcerated people.

While providing forced labor, immigrants lack many of the labor protections available to traditional employees and lack the resources to draw attention to the injustices they face. Detainees are also at risk of experiencing medical neglect, inadequate food, and overcrowded, filthy quarters. This abysmal situation has led to strikes at detention centers across the country.

Cracking down on immigrants is in direct opposition to Trump’s promise of a “golden age of America.” Ample research demonstrates that immigrants are less likely to commit crime; increase the size of the labor force and gross domestic production, which positively impacts the economy; and contribute more taxes than they receive in public benefits. But while immigrant workers are crucial to stabilizing the economy, increased enforcement is causing a decline in the labor market and will inevitably restrict local and national economies.

Taking a Page Out of the Mass Incarceration Playbook

What the Trump Administration and ICE are doing is not new. Increasing detention by targeting immigrant communities is part of a long history of unethically extracting profit from marginalized communities.

Recent narratives around immigrant fraud, inflated public benefit consumption, and criminality mobilized to justify the actions of ICE, Customs and Border Protection, and the Department of Homeland Security mirror racist tropes about the “welfare queen,” inner-city violence, and inherent criminality of Black people. Those and other stereotypes were used to both legitimize restrictions on federal assistance programs that most affected working Black families and justify building the carceral infrastructure needed to fulfill “tough on crime” policy agendas. Even the images of immigrant parents being kidnapped and children getting pepper sprayed or tear gassed that have become common over the last year bear a striking resemblance to the media coverage that surrounds police killings of Black people.

To make matters worse, the Supreme Court has given law enforcement the green light to racially profile immigrants, thus enabling an environment of fear and risk that normalizes armed agents harassing people based on how they look and speak, what they are wearing, and where they work. Findings from a CLASP study on how current immigration operations have harmed immigrant families and early education and child care providers corroborate the implementation of an immigration enforcement model based on discrimination and anti-Blackness. The study included interviews with immigrants and providers who compared the environment of heightened discrimination, risk, and fear they were navigating to the racism and police violence experienced by Black people in the U.S.

Far-Reaching Consequences The Trump Administration’s decision to greatly expand immigrant detention does more than remove immigrant workers from their jobs and families. It transfers public resources to the agencies and contractors that confine people while creating a captive population available to perform labor for nominal compensation. Consequently, immigrant communities bear the brunt of lost wages, family separation, care disruptions, and economic instability, while detention operators receive public resources and reduced operating costs.

These impacts have spread far beyond industries predominantly occupied by immigrants. As of May 2026, over 668,000 jobs have been lost as a result of the chilling effects generated by anti-immigrant activities. The human cost is high as well. In addition to the thousands of lives that have been disrupted and hundreds of families separated, at least 52 people have died in ICE custody since January 2025.

Investing in the destruction of immigrant communities is not a strategy for national safety nor economic security. Rather than financing a system that removes workers from local economies and their families and extracts value from them in custody, policymakers should invest in the conditions that allow families and communities to thrive, such as programs that help everyone afford the daily costs of living, like child care, nutrition assistance, and health care. Policies that support immigrants support us all.

text:
A California federal judge held the Trump Administration in civil contempt for violating a court order requiring them to forensically image personal phones used by agents present at 15 identified immigration operations.

U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong ordered the government to pay $500 per day until they fully comply with a January 16 order from a magistrate judge regarding the imaging of the phones.

“Upon review of the parties’ submissions and counsel’s representations at the hearing, it does not appear that Defendants’ noncompliance is due to an inability to comply,” Frimpong said in her order. “Instead, the clear and convincing evidence shows that Defendants have acted intentionally and not in good faith.

The Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A Justice Department lawyer filed a notice indicating the government had submitted a $3,500 payment on Tuesday.

Frimpong’s July 28 order, which was unsealed Tuesday, stems from a class action lawsuit filed last year by the American Civil Liberties Union of Southern California, Public Counsel, other groups and private attorneys calling to end unlawful stops and arrests and for the protection of due process and access to counsel rights for people in immigration detention.

As part of the lawsuit, U.S. Magistrate Judge Sheri Pym had ordered the government in January to forensically image any cell phones used by agents during specific operations. In May, the plaintiffs in the case asked the court to order the government to prove why they should not be held in contempt over the failure to image a single personal phone since Pym’s order.

Frimpong, an appointee of President Biden, ordered the government to reimburse the plaintiffs and organizations that brought the lawsuit for the time and costs spent “in getting the Government to comply with the Magistrate Judge’s Order.”

“Not only are federal agents violating the Constitution on the streets, the government is violating court orders by intentionally withholding critical evidence about its immigration enforcement operations. The court has found the government in contempt and rightfully issued sanctions,” said Mayra Joachín, senior staff attorney with the ACLU Foundation of Southern California. “We cannot allow the government’s disturbing pattern of unlawful conduct and misleading public statements about its immigration operations to continue.”

The plaintiffs also noted in the May filing that the government had informed them that Gregory Bovino, the former commander at large for Border Patrol, had lost his previously issued work phone in January 2026 and was issued a new phone.

At a June 25 contempt hearing, Jonathan Robbins, a Justice Department lawyer, said they objected to the order regarding personal phones, stating that those “are not in our custody and control.”

Robbins told the judge that U.S. Customs and Border Protection had sent questionnaires to agents associated with Operation at Large Los Angeles, with more than 1,400 returned. Of those, 885 officers indicated they use their personal phones for work, according to Robbins.

Although 88 agents consented to the forensic imaging of their personal phones, Robbins said none of those had been imaged at the time of the hearing.

Robbins said government phones were still being imaged at that point, with a capacity for only three phones every two weeks. He told the judge it was “a very, very slow process.”

“It’s a completely overly intrusive way to collect discovery,” Robbins told Frimpong, noting that agents who had been deployed to L.A. were now scattered across the country. “We’re not trying to flout the orders of the court.”

“We’re over four months later and all I’m hearing is that an email and a questionnaire went out,” Frimpong said during the hearing. “We’re not going to wait forever.”

During the hearing, David Fry of Munger Tolles & Olson, which is representing the plaintiffs, told Frimpong that the imaging of the phones was a meaningful measure to address concerns that some agents may not be following the rules. Fry noted that racially insensitive comments had been found in some materials.

text:
(CN) — The European Union’s harsh new legal framework against migration — the source of fierce disagreement between Europe’s right and left — came into sharp focus Tuesday at an emergency meeting following last week’s deadly storming of Spain’s heavily guarded colonial-era exclave of Ceuta on the coast of Morocco.

Over two days of chaos, dozens of people, mostly young Moroccan men, died as they tried to swim across bays, climb barbed-wire fences and breach gates around Ceuta. Many drowned or were crushed in stampedes, authorities said. Investigations are underway by Spanish authorities.

A lot remains unclear about what led more than 70,000 people to storm Ceuta, a fortified Spanish city of about 80,000 people on the African side of the Strait of Gibraltar.

It is one of two Spanish exclaves in North Africa that have long been the scene of clashes between border agents and migrants seeking to force their way past fences as a route into the European Union. Adding to tensions, Morocco claims the cities as its own.

But last week’s storming was by far the largest ever and left Spanish border agents unable to stop the mass of people.

For about 48 hours between late Thursday and Saturday, Ceuta was overwhelmed as the intruders took over parks, boulevards and stores.

Over the weekend, Spain deployed large military contingents to patrol the city and bring it back under control. About 200 people who breached Ceuta’s fences remained under processing for asylum, though they were mostly boys and young men protected from expulsion by their status as unaccompanied minors.

By Tuesday, the death toll had risen to at least 83, according to the Associated Press. The AP said 72 bodies were recovered on the Spanish side of Ceuta’s 5-mile border with Morocco.

So far, Spanish authorities have limited themselves to blaming human traffickers, but experts believe other actors, including Morocco’s officialdom, may have been involved in stoking the mayhem for cynical political reasons.

The fallout from last week’s dramatic events have proved very damaging to Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, one of Europe’s last remaining left-leaning leaders amid a surge in conservative and far-right parties in most EU countries.

His grip on power was already under immense strain due to corruption probes and a right-wing opposition gelling into a formidable force. Only last week, Spain’s center-right Popular Party announced it was open to reversing a policy against governing with Spain’s ultra-nationalist far-right Vox party.

Speaking to reporters in Brussels, the European Commission’s top official for migration said the events in Ceuta underscored the need to do even more to seal the bloc’s borders against “illegal migration.”

His comments came amid acrimonious debates over the extent to which the EU should safeguard the lives and rights of people seeking refuge from poverty, war, climate change, persecution and disease.

Conceived in the aftermath of the horrors of World War II, the European Union was engineered in a manner to become a beacon of human rights. But that aspiration has been gravely weakened by the bloc’s stone-cold attitude toward migrant deaths in the past decade, its cooperation with authoritarian regimes and more recent refusal to punish Israel for its wide-scale human rights violations in occupied Palestinian territories.

In June, Europe began enforcing a harsher migration regime that grants authorities sweeping powers to arrest and deport migrants and set up camps outside the bloc where migrants can be processed. Many human rights experts say the laws do not comply with international standards to protect the vulnerable.

The so-called Pact on Migration and Asylum has not been vetted yet by the EU’s top courts and parts of it could be reversed.

Far-right Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni played a big role in getting the tougher laws passed after she seized power in Rome following the coronavirus pandemic. Meloni, like others on Europe’s extreme right, has long railed against immigration from Muslim countries as an existential threat to Italy and Europe’s Christian values.

She’s gone further than others in blocking humanitarian vessels from bringing rescued migrants to Italy and she broke a taboo by establishing special camps for migrants in Albania.

The legality of her Albania experiment remains contested with the European Court of Justice, the EU’s top court, sending signals that it may uphold them as permissible under EU law. The new pact was written in part to legalize the use of processing centers outside the EU.

The far-right’s version of migration as fundamentally baleful to Europe has fused with a common public apprehension that migration is transforming Europe into unrecognizably violent multi-ethnic societies.

In the wake of the assault on Ceuta, politicians across a surprising number of parties and countries lambasted Sánchez as partly responsible for the disaster in Ceuta due to his embrace of immigrants.

Last month, Sánchez’s left-wing coalition government went against the anti-immigrant trend by opening a path to citizenship for more than 1 million people living in Spain without a residency permit. Most of those eligible are from Latin America.

On Tuesday, Magnus Brunner, the EU commissioner for migration, also took aim at Sánchez.

“I do understand that with the images we saw, the citizens of Europe were concerned,” Brunner told reporters following the emergency meeting.

He said there was broad agreement across the EU that the provisions in the new migration pact should be carried out swiftly.

He touted so-called “return hubs,” expedited border screenings and asylum processing centers outside the EU as the next steps to rein in mass migration.

However, many experts warn these policies run foul of international asylum protections and warn Europe is turning its back on a core mission to uphold human rights.

The mood in Brussels though is definitely toughening.

In a rare rebuke from a European Commission official toward a national leader, Brunner called out Sánchez for his amnesty law for immigrants living off the books.

“It’s not a good signal for the rest of Europe,” he said.

He said the Ceuta crisis was a “test of our European resilience” and “security of our external borders.”

“For the time being, Europe I think has definitely passed this test,” he said. “People did not manage to enter the Schengen area.”

He was referring to the EU’s core principle that borders within the bloc must remain open to cross free of border checks. Schengen is a border town in Luxembourg where European leaders in 1985 signed an agreement to do away with border checks to facilitate the movement of goods and people.

Brunner praised Europe for cracking down on immigration.

“The numbers show this,” he said. “Illegal migration decreased by 55% last year and it’s [down by] 40% this year.”

About 49,000 people have crossed EU borders this year without permission, a massive drop from 2015 when about 1 million people, most them fleeing the Syrian civil war, marched across European borders in search of refuge.

He said the number of people entering the EU without permission this year was “roughly about the same as one week in the Greek islands in October 2015.”

“By every measure, Europe has not had this much control over illegal migration in decades,” he said.

Over the weekend, 22 of the EU’s 27 member states signed a letter criticizing Sánchez for his migrant amnesty.

Courthouse News reporter Cain Burdeau is based in the European Union.

text:
HIGHLAND PARK — On the lawn of the Reformed Church of Highland Park Tuesday, nearly 100 people rallied to call for the closure of Newark migrant jail Delaney Hall after the death of a 39-year-old man in ICE custody Saturday.

Edwin Jovanny Lopez Cornejo’s family made pleas to Gov. Mikie Sherrill and the Attorney General’s Office to investigate his death and called for the release of his medical records, while urging the federal government to cease the detention of undocumented immigrants. Cornejo was detained at Delaney Hall for six weeks before his death.

“I’m going to grow up without a father,” said Ashley, Cornejo’s 12-year-old daughter. “They didn’t even let him see me one last time before he died.”

For roughly two hours, the crowd in front of the church prayed, chanted for the closure of Delaney Hall, and heard stories from people who have loved ones held at the Newark detention center.

Cornejo was a Salvadoran immigrant who lived in the U.S. for more than 20 years, according to his family. They said he had diabetes and high blood pressure and was not being given his medication regularly since he had been detained June 18. His mother said she has still not been contacted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials or Geo Group, the private company that runs Delaney Hall.

ICE, which said Cornejo was deported in 2006 after crossing the border illegally, stated that Cornejo received “proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals” while in custody. His official cause of death is still pending.

His brother disputes that Cornejo was receiving the medical attention he needed, noting he was on daily medication. Cornejo told his brother in jail phone calls that to get Tylenol for a headache, he had to fill out a form, and often wouldn’t receive it for two or three days.

“Nothing will bring back my brother,” he said in Spanish. “It’s not right, everything that happened. And no one knows, no one speaks up because of fear, but sometimes we need to lose our fear to get justice.”

Jenny Garcia, an activist with American Friends Service Committee, said that Delaney Hall detainees have complained about being given the wrong medication or being told they have to split medication because there isn’t enough for everyone. She alleged that ICE is not being truthful about whether detainees are seen by doctors or given the medicine they need.

Maribel Encalada said her dad is one of those people who is denied medical care. Her 58-year-old father, who came to the U.S. over 40 years ago, has been in detention for several weeks. He’s been denied medical attention for his high blood pressure and a painful toothache that’s developed since he arrived at the jail, she said. He’s also been fed moldy bread, she said.

“Every day that he is denied proper medical care is another day that his health is put at risk,” she said. “Access to basic medical treatment is not a privilege, it’s a basic human right — and my father’s story is not the only one.”

Cornejo’s death comes amid a rising death toll in ICE custody nationally. At least 22 ICE detainees have died in the first seven months of the year, according to the agency’s national data. At this point in 2025, ICE had reported 12 in-custody deaths.

Up until June, ICE policy required the agency to report deaths of detainees who die within 30 days of being released from custody, but it now no longer does. Advocates said the change makes it harder to track deaths tied to medical neglect that surfaces after someone is released or transferred.

Several activists expressed concerns about whether there could be more deaths linked to Delaney Hall than ICE has reported publicly.

After an unannounced visit to the jail Monday, Rep. Rob Menendez (D-08) said that in July, a person who was being processed at Delaney Hall was having a medical episode when ICE released them from custody, and they later died at University Hospital in Newark. His office said it is working to learn more about the circumstances of the death and other medical emergencies that have occurred inside the facility, noting an ambulance was on site Monday morning.

An unsigned statement from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, said all immigrant detainees are provided with medical care and downplayed in-custody deaths as just “0.008% of the detained population.”

“As bed space has rapidly expanded, we have maintained higher a standard of care than most prisons that hold U.S. citizens — including providing access to proper medical care. For many illegal aliens this is the best healthcare they have received their entire lives,” the statement reads. “Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $2,600 and a free flight to self-deport now.”

Sally Pillay, a longtime volunteer with Eyes on ICE, on Tuesday called detention centers “death camps.”

“We have so many people right now in immigration custody at Delaney Hall who have been detained for over a year in that facility, who have medical issues, medical concerns. We have a number of individuals who are diabetic, who are not getting their medications in time, and they are not getting food,” Pillay said.

She said she’s “pleading and begging” lawmakers to help get medically vulnerable people out of detention as soon as possible.

Rep. Analilia Mejia (D-11), who said her mother was once undocumented, called on ICE to be abolished. Mejia urged her colleagues to continue to visit the detention centers, press federal officials, and enter all that they discover into the congressional record.

“I will do my part, you will do your part, and I know that together we will demand and we will win the kind of justice that, sadly, Edwin was not given,” she said. “Shut it down.”

text:
Washington - The family of a man from El Salvador, who died in a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center in New Jersey, alleged medical negligence during his custody and demanded an independent investigation into his death.

ICE said on Monday that Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, who was being held at the Delaney Hall detention facility, was pronounced dead on Saturday by medical personnel at University Hospital, in Newark, New Jersey, after suffering what the agency described as a medical emergency.

Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Lopez-Cornejo's family said he suffered from a number of underlying health conditions including high blood pressure, diabetes and epilepsy, and relied on several medications to keep those conditions under control.

His mother, Maria Cornejo, said he called a day before his death and told her he lost feeling in half his face and arm.

"My son needed medical attention, and he did not receive it," his mother said in Spanish. His 12-year-old daughter also alleged he was denied medications and that he had lost a lot of weight in custody.

Lopez-Cornejo's death comes amid broader scrutiny of conditions in U.S. immigration detention facilities. More than 50 people have died in ICE custody nationwide since President Donald Trump took office in January last year, while rights groups have repeatedly raised concerns about medical care and living conditions at the facilities.

ICE said Lopez-Cornejo received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals.

"When Lopez-Cornejo experienced a medical emergency while in ICE custody, GEO facility staff and medical staff responded immediately and called 911 for emergency medical services. The official cause of death remains pending further medical examination," ICE said in a statement on Monday.

The agency reiterated that statement when asked for comment on the remarks by Lopez-Cornejo's family.

Inspection

While the family demanded an independent investigation into the death, New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill said her administration continues to "face obstruction in our efforts to conduct a full health inspection of the facility."

ICE has dismissed reports of poor conditions and maintained that it takes seriously the safety and health of detainees.

ICE has been at the center of Trump's immigration crackdown and deportation drive that rights groups condemn as violating free speech and due process rights.

Human rights advocates also say the crackdown has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

Trump says his actions aim to improve domestic security.

title: Ceuta was a carnival of anti-migrant content for hateful opportunists on the right - The Guardian
description:
Why was the migrant incursion at Ceuta, on the Spanish-Moroccan border, such a big story across the world?
What made it an irresistible front-page story in the Daily Mail, the Daily Express and the Daily Telegraph?
“About 48,000 of the up to 60,000 people who came into Ceuta from Morocco returned within a day.
The European Union has spent years, and hundreds of millions of euros, on developing partnerships with Morocco on border management.
And frankly, when the next Ceuta happens, the left needs to think of a better response than simply being thankful they went home again.
text:
The live streams are still running, training their cameras on the beach at Ceuta, where nothing is happening. The self-styled citizen journalists are still pounding the streets, capturing their shaky smartphone footage. Zia Yusuf of Reform UK was out there at the weekend, wearing a crisp white shirt and smart tailored trousers, lest anyone confuse him with the other brown people there. The bad brown people.

Why was the migrant incursion at Ceuta, on the Spanish-Moroccan border, such a big story across the world? How did it manage to pique the interest of Donald Trump and Elon Musk, to feature on NBC’s Nightly News, not – shall we say – a programme massively predisposed to spotlighting news stories from continental Africa? What about it so exercised Europe’s heads of government? What made it an irresistible front-page story in the Daily Mail, the Daily Express and the Daily Telegraph?

Certainly not any kind of urgent or imminent threat to our own borders, much less the borders of the United States. The Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla operate under special exemptions from the Schengen area, rendering it almost impossible for an undocumented migrant to reach mainland Spain, about 12 miles away across the Mediterranean. Once many of the migrants realised this, they duly left.

Nor any kind of humanitarian concern for those who drowned or were killed in the crowd crush. “About 48,000 of the up to 60,000 people who came into Ceuta from Morocco returned within a day. Still, the sudden influx created a crisis for Spain’s pro-immigration government. Nearly three dozen died.” So read a New York Times subheading on Friday. And once you fight your way past the tortured syntax, did you notice anything unusual there? First the integrity of the border, then the political ramifications, then the people who died: the hierarchy of rightwing immigration discourse expressed in three perfect sentences. The death toll has since risen to either 72 or 88 – authorities disagree on the number – and nobody seems over-fussed either way.

Rather, Ceuta functions as a kind of border porn for the global far right: a locus upon which to project their most vivid and apocalyptic fantasies. If the historian Mike Davis once described the US-Mexico border wall as “a political stage set”, then in the age of the deepfake and the troll-farm, Ceuta has proved a similarly fertile source of content: the border interface reimagined as digital theatre, mass migration as primetime television.

The rich irony here is that from a securitisation standpoint, Ceuta functions almost exactly as it was intended. A six metre-high barbed-wire fence, reinforced by watchtowers and a network of video cameras, separates it from Morocco. From Ceuta, an internal checkpoint guards the only ferry route to mainland Spain. The European Union has spent years, and hundreds of millions of euros, on developing partnerships with Morocco on border management.

None of which seemed to matter in the slightest as European leaders queued up to give the Pedro Sánchez government a ritual horse-whipping. Italy reintroduced air and sea border controls with Spain. Emmanuel Macron deployed mobile units to the Spanish border to strengthen controls. Giorgia Meloni – backed by Finland, Denmark and Czechia – has argued that Spain’s membership of the Schengen area should be suspended.

And of course these are primarily domestic politicians catering to a domestic market, ahead of an electoral cycle in which incumbents in France, Italy and Poland are being outflanked by nativist insurgents to their right. Sánchez himself faces the ballot box in 2027, an election in which his government can boast strong economic growth and which his rightwing opponents will therefore be desperate to turn into a referendum on immigration.

So that’s the political angle. But really the spectacle of Ceuta represents a more primal and guttural need, particularly in the English-speaking world, for the inflammatory anti-immigration crusade to be seen as well as spoken. The photos and footage coming out of the enclave in recent days, all shot from distance and almost never in closeup, are all geared towards a single end: to encourage the viewer to see these brown bodies as a single mass, each indistinguishable from the other, the accountants and surgeons from the bomb-makers and rapists, the living from the dead.

And so, by small degrees, the line between nationalism and pure-blood white supremacy blurs a little more. Indeed, the very idea that a single border crossing 1,000 miles and two seas away from us is somehow our urgent problem, only really makes sense in a worldview whose real distinction is not between “Britain” and “abroad” but between an imagined white Christian Europe and a savage brown other.

For all this, the right does not act alone. The palpable relief on many parts of the left as most of the original 60,000 migrants returned to Morocco spoke of a worrying acquiescence: a tacit acceptance of the dangerous trope of migration as a prima facie problem. Here’s a radical thought: what if migration is only a problem to those who want it to be? What if we started seeing the mass movement of people less as an existential threat and more as a simple inevitability of human existence? Nine years ago the great Gary Younge set out in the Guardian a utopian vision of open borders and no immigration controls. What happened to that sense of vision and idealism? When did border discourse, the conversation on why and how we move, become something to be feared and not embraced?

Whether Ceuta was an accidental security lapse or a deliberately engineered event is actually beside the point. The point is that as the global right grows in confidence, as the migration industrial complex thirsts for new content, new border porn, there will be more Ceutas in the future. People will keep migrating and die trying, and because this is good telly it will keep happening. “Today more than ever,” writes the sociologist Mimi Sheller in her book Mobility Justice, “these borderlands are soaked in the blood of white nationalism, ethnic profiling, and enforced death in the no man’s land.”

The endgame here is massacres, vigilante violence, not “stop the boats” but shoot the boats, the border reimagined as a computer-game war zone. The endgame is what the likes of Musk and his far-right meat puppets are already depicting: a world where zombie armies of “military-age males” invade our virgin turf, and the problem is not the forces that drove them from their homes, but your “suicidal empathy”, because these are not equal humans deserving equal treatment. These are the stakes. And frankly, when the next Ceuta happens, the left needs to think of a better response than simply being thankful they went home again.

text:
California’s legal campaign against the Trump administration has preserved more than $200 billion in threatened federal funding, Attorney General Rob Bonta said Tuesday. During the first 18 months of President Donald Trump’s second term, the state filed 82 lawsuits and submitted 120 friend-of-the-court briefs in other cases.

The actions ranged from lawsuits to claw back funds frozen by the Republican administration over political differences with the state’s Democratic leaders to efforts to defend California’s environmental laws. Cases challenged President Donald Trump’s orders to end birthright citizenship, restrict mail-in voting and defund Planned Parenthood. The state also challenged the presence of National Guard troops in Los Angeles and Portland amid protests over the president’s immigration crackdowns.

The state also defended itself in court. Responding to 11 lawsuits filed by the federal government, California’s attorneys fought allegations ranging from efforts to end in-state tuition for undocumented students to claims that a law meant to ensure humane treatment of chickens led to higher egg prices.

“Since President Trump returned to office, California has been under attack — and has led the way in fighting back,” Bonta said Tuesday. “We’ve protected funding that keeps our communities safe, feeds hungry families, and ensures our kids get the education they deserve. We’ve gone all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court to defend constitutional rights — and won.”

Bonta’s office drew down an auxiliary state fund appropriated for such actions by more than $19 million during the 2025-26 fiscal year, the attorney general said in a report to the Legislature also released Tuesday. But those funds — which came on top of the roughly $17 million appropriated by the Legislature for such lawsuits — were not nearly enough to cover the full cost, Bonta said in the report.

“The $19.2 million in ... funds that the Department has received to date has contributed to — but in no way has been sufficient to cover — the costs of the litigation,” the report said.

The 82 lawsuits filed since Trump began his second term in January 2025 amount to just over one per week, marking a roughly 25% increase over the more than 60 actions the state had taken by March 2026. In addition to the lawsuits and amicus briefs, California also issued 112 comment letters, formal responses to proposed changes in federal policy.

The report, which covered lawsuits filed through July 23, reported 79 cases, but Bonta’s office said Tuesday the number had already risen to 82.

The work was intensive. State lawyers and their coworkers spent 154,000 hours on the cases during the first nine months of 2025 alone, according to previous Bee reporting. That is equivalent to about 99 full-time employees.

The expenditures were worth it, Bonta said, because the state recovered billions in funding that had been frozen or threatened by the federal government.

Those funds included $5 billion for childcare and family assistance, $8.7 billion in agricultural grants, $1 billion for emergency preparedness and $55 million for public safety efforts related to terrorism, the report said. Legal efforts also recovered $7.7 billion in transportation funding and $5 billion for education, Bonta said. [Remove stray bracket.]

The state appears well on its way to exceeding the 120 lawsuits then-Attorney General Xavier Becerra, now the Democratic candidate for governor, filed against the federal government during the first Trump administration.

The report drew a sharp response from White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson, who used a pejorative misspelling of Gov. Gavin Newsom’s name to emphasize her point.

“Instead of bragging about filing frivolous lawsuits against the Trump Administration, the California AG should focus on addressing problems in his own state – like the countless criminal illegal aliens the Newscum Administration allows to roam free and terrorize communities,” Jackson said in an email.

California is one of several Democratic-led states that have repeatedly sued the federal government under Trump and other Republican administrations.

Republican-led states likewise have frequently sued Democratic administrations.

During the administration of former President Joe Biden, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, now a candidate for the U.S. Senate, filed 100 lawsuits challenging the administration’s policies.

After Trump was re-elected in 2024, the California Legislature set aside $25 million for legal action against the federal government, to be used in addition to general fund appropriations to the state Department of Justice. Most or all of that money has already been used.

On Tuesday, Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, D-Hollister, said the money was well spent.

“That $25 million has protected an estimated $207 billion for the people of California,” Rivas said in a statement. “That isn’t politics. That’s responsible government.”

text:
The Department of Health and Human Services quietly unveiled a multimillion-dollar contract Tuesday with a small Texas law firm, entrusting it with representing thousands of children who came by themselves to the United States during immigration court proceedings.

Per a notice set to be officially published in the Federal Register on Thursday, but posted to the website Tuesday, the Office of Refugee Resettlement, the division of HHS that oversees the well-being of unaccompanied minors, will award Burke Law Group, a Houston-based law firm, a contract worth up to $150 million a year.

Burke Law Group will “provide legal orientation, legal consultation, and attorney-of-record representation services for eligible unaccompanied alien children during immigration proceedings.”

The contract will run through August of next year and will replace the existing plan for representing unaccompanied children. Until Friday, ORR had a contract with the Acacia Center for Justice, but the federal government allowed that contract to expire after months of withholding funds to Acacia, and by extension, many of the nonprofits that served as “subcontractors” and represented the majority of the children in ORR care.

Acacia and its subcontractors — which included major nonprofits such as Kids in Need of Defense as well as smaller community-based nonprofits — have represented nearly 20,000 children.

Now that responsibility will fall on a law firm with 26 employees spread across eight offices. The firm bills itself as a “boutique” firm “known for elite counsel in high-stakes litigation, environmental, regulatory, and corporate matters.” None of the lawyers for the firm list immigration law as an area of expertise, per a POLITICO review of the firm’s site.

The Burke Law Group did not immediately respond to a voicemail requesting comment.

The federal government under the provisions of a 2008 anti-human trafficking law is required to facilitate access to legal counsel for children who came to the United States by themselves. For decades, a series of nonprofits — first the Vera Institute for Justice and then Acacia — covered those needs.

But the Trump administration has had a fractious relationship with the nonprofits. In 2025, HHS first moved to cancel the contracts outright, though that effort stalled due to litigation. The administration at the end of 2025 then began withholding payment from the nonprofits after demanding that they share sensitive information about their clients with the federal government.

At the end of 2025, ORR had announced it was soliciting bids for law firms and other entities to take on the obligation of representing unaccompanied children amid its dispute with Acacia.

The contract — a single-source cooperative agreement — should in theory allow for other law firms or nonprofit legal defense groups to serve as subcontractors, though that will occur at the discretion of the Burke Law Group.

text:
By Kanishka Singh

WASHINGTON, Aug 4 (Reuters) – The family of a man from El Salvador, who died in a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center in New Jersey, alleged medical negligence during his custody and demanded an ​independent investigation into his death.

ICE said on Monday that Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, who ‌was being held at the Delaney Hall detention facility, was pronounced dead on Saturday by medical personnel at University Hospital, in Newark, New Jersey, after suffering what the agency described as a medical emergency.

Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Lopez-Cornejo’s family said he suffered from a number of underlying ‌health ​conditions including high blood pressure, diabetes and epilepsy, and ⁠relied on several medications to keep ⁠those conditions under control.

His mother, Maria Cornejo, said he called a day before his death and told her he lost feeling in half his face and arm.

“My son needed medical attention, and he did not receive it,” his mother said ​in Spanish. His 12-year-old daughter also alleged he was denied medications and that he had lost a lot of weight in custody.

Lopez-Cornejo’s death comes amid broader scrutiny ⁠of conditions in U.S. immigration detention facilities. More ⁠than 50 people have died in ICE custody nationwide since President ​Donald Trump took office in January last year, while rights groups have repeatedly raised concerns ​about medical care and living conditions at the facilities.

ICE said Lopez-Cornejo received ‌proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals.

“When Lopez-Cornejo experienced a medical emergency while in ICE custody, GEO facility staff and medical staff responded immediately and called 911 for emergency medical services. The official cause of death remains pending further medical examination,” ICE ⁠said in a statement on Monday.

The agency reiterated that statement when asked for comment on the remarks by Lopez-Cornejo’s family.

INSPECTION

While the family demanded an independent investigation into the death, ⁠New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill ‌said her administration continues to “face obstruction in our efforts to ⁠conduct a full health inspection of the facility.”

ICE has dismissed reports ​of ‌poor conditions and maintained that it takes seriously the safety ​and health of ⁠detainees.

ICE has been at the center of Trump’s immigration crackdown and deportation drive that rights groups condemn as violating free speech and due process rights.

Human rights advocates also say the crackdown has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

Trump says his actions aim to improve domestic security.

(Reporting by Kanishka Singh in Washington; ​Editing by Sanjeev Miglani)
